September 19, 2025 · Washington D.C. · Shared with Public The Senate voted 47–43 on Friday to confirm Michael Waltz as U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, filling the last remaining seat in President Trump’s Cabinet. Sen. Rand Paul (KY) was the lone Republican to vote against, while three Democrats voted in favor: Sens. John Fetterman (PA), Mark Kelly (AZ) and Jeanne Shaheen (NH). Mr. Waltz, a former Florida congressman, was nominated for the U.N. post after his dismissal as national security adviser on May 1, being replaced by Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Quora Question In the US,  how many Senate votes  are needed  to confirm  a presidential cabinet nominee? Can the majority leader prevent such  a vote  from being scheduled? Answer   ·  12 votes A majority of the votes is required for approval of a cabinet pick. The exact number depends on how many are voting. In the case of a tie the Vice President votes as president of the Senate.

And yes, the filibuster rule is in effect and it tales 60 votes to force a vote on a nominee.

I should note that there are relatively few confirmed cabinet secretaries right now, with most of them in “acting” roles. There is a statute, the Federal Vacancies Act of 1998, [1] that gives the president some flexibility in cases when a nominee is before the Senate and they do not act.

1. Federal Vacancies Reform Act of 1998 - Wikipedia [ https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Vacancies_Reform_Act_of_1998 ] More Quora Question Why should a 60-vote threshold in the US  Senate  be needed for  confirming ambassadors  but not Supreme Court appointees? Answer   ·  79 votes So you misunderstand the Filibuster rule...allow me to explain it to you....it takes a bit, so strap in...

It's not that a piece of legislation requires 60 votes to be passed, 51 will do. It's that the Senate's Rules Of Order allow for two things:

1. Any Senator has an absolute right to be heard to speak on the floor regarding any measure being considered

2. A Senator is allowed to speak for as long as they wish, and their speech does not have to be germane to the subject of the bill

So, combining those two rules, we see that it is theoretically possible for any Senator to decide for him or herself that they are so opposed to a measure that they will speak, forever, in order to prevent it's passage.

This is at it's heart what a filibuster is...it's just a particular Senator being willing to say "I am so against this I am going to stand on the floor and talk forever, preventing anything from getting done, until this is made to go away"
